Qualified is a versatile tool that serves multiple purposes. It is an AI-powered sales and marketing platform that handles sponsor inquiries, attendee questions, and lead qualification. Additionally, it is a sales engagement platform used for adding AI-qualified leads to sequences and triggering automated follow-up sequences. The platform's AI AEs (Artificial Intelligence Agents) automate and optimize sales processes, making it an essential tool for businesses seeking to streamline their sales operations.

chunks.content: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former. But when you raise

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects

The Uncomfortable Truth About Jobs
Jason is refreshingly direct: AI is displacing midpack and mediocre sales professionals. Not the best, not (yet) leadership—but the middle of the pack is getting squeezed.
The media narrative of “mass layoffs” is mostly wrong, though. What’s actually happening is more subtle: companies are backfilling roles with AI instead of hiring humans. The job that would have gone to a new SDR now goes to an AI agent. The headcount just never gets added.
For salespeople, the advice is clear: Don’t wait. Pick an AI tool today. Train it yourself. Become the person at your company who knows how to make AI agents productive. That skill set is the new job security.
